tldr: G-Memory is a hierarchical graph-based memory system for multi-agent systems that manages lengthy inter-agent collaboration via three-tier graph structures (insight, query, and interaction graphs), enabling cross-trial knowledge reuse and self-evolution. Experiments show improvements of up to 20.89% in embodied action and 10.12% in knowledge QA accuracy.
contributions: Identification of the bottleneck in self-evolving capabilities of MAS attributed to oversimplified memory architectures
Proposal of G-Memory, a plug-and-play hierarchical agentic memory architecture for MAS using insight, query, and interaction graphs
Extensive experimental evaluation across five benchmarks, three LLM backbones, and three MAS frameworks demonstrating superior performance and resource efficiency
methods: G-Memory manages MAS interaction history through a three-tier hierarchical graph structure: (1) Insight Graph stores distilled generalizable insights with supporting query sets, (2) Query Graph encodes task queries with metadata (status, difficulty) and semantic connections, and (3) Interaction Graph stores fine-grained agent utterance trajectories. Upon a new query, it performs coarse-grained similarity-based retrieval on the query graph followed by hop expansion, then executes bi-directional traversal: upward to retrieve high-level insights and downward to extract core interaction subgraphs via an LLM-facilitated sparsifier. Each agent receives role-specific memory augmentation. After task execution, the hierarchy is updated by assimilating new trajectories, insights, and query connections based on environmental feedback.
results: G-Memory improves success rates by up to 20.89% on embodied action tasks and 10.12% on knowledge QA tasks across five benchmarks, three LLM backbones, and three MAS frameworks (AutoGen, DyLAN, ComplexCoT/CoT). It maintains comparable or lower token usage than mainstream memory designs. The system achieves these gains without any modifications to the original frameworks, demonstrating its plug-and-play capability.
limitations: Existing MAS memory mechanisms are overly simplistic, disregarding nuanced inter-agent collaboration trajectories
Cross-trial memory in prior work remains rudimentary, typically only transmitting condensed artifacts (final solutions) rather than meaningful collaborative experience
Naive feeding of entire long-context trajectories without proper abstraction poses challenges for traditional retrieval-based memory designs
Transfer of single-agent memory mechanisms to MAS is not straightforward due to substantially longer task-solving trajectories (up to 10x more tokens)
